03 / Batting room

Batters who absorb pressure.

The batter score rewards high-pressure strike rate, low dot-ball percentage, lower dismissal rate and strike-rate retention versus baseline.

PROVISIONAL TOP 10
Batting score composition: 40% high-pressure strike-rate percentile + 25% inverse dot-ball percentile + 20% inverse dismissal-rate percentile + 15% strike-rate change versus baseline percentile. Reliability adjustment = raw score × √min(high-pressure balls / 180, 1).

05 / Methodology

From ball-by-ball to shortlist.

The model is intentionally interpretable. Each stage is designed to be auditable and explainable to a scouting panel.

◉

01. Define pressure

Innings progression = legal balls elapsed before delivery / scheduled legal balls × 100. Wicket stress = wickets lost before delivery / 10 × 100. Pressure Index = 50% progression + 50% wicket stress.

▥

02. Segment innings

Low: 0–25. Moderate: >25–50. High: >50–75. Extreme: >75–100. High pressure means PI >50. Innings 1 and 2 included; Super Overs excluded.

⌁

03. Apply eligibility

Batters: at least 60 high-pressure balls and 30 baseline balls. Bowlers: at least 100 high-pressure legal-ball proxies and 30 baseline legal-ball proxies.

✦

04. Score batters

40% HP strike-rate percentile, 25% inverse dot-ball percentile, 20% inverse dismissal-rate percentile, 15% SR-change percentile. Then apply exposure reliability adjustment.

⚑

05. Score bowlers

50% HP wickets per 100 legal-ball proxies, 20% wicket-rate lift, 15% inverse boundary-concession rate, 15% HP dot-ball proxy. Then apply exposure reliability adjustment.

↻

06. Stress-test

Batter robustness tested across pressure thresholds, progression/wicket weights and minimum exposure. Top-10 overlap varied from 5 to 10 across six reported scenarios.

Dataset coverage: 853 target matches; 837 with ball-by-ball coverage and 16 without. 193,988 regulation-innings deliveries were processed. Revised-target data was sparse; full innings totals and bowler economy were not reconstructed.
06 / Data integrity

What this model does not claim.

A useful scouting tool should be transparent about uncertainty. These are the boundaries of this analysis snapshot.

Key limitations

1

Source semantics

No complete data dictionary was supplied. extras1_runs appears categorical and extras_2_runs semantics are unresolved.

2

Bowling economy

Runs conceded and economy were not reconstructed. The bowling list is wicket-focused and exploratory only.

3

Pressure proxy

No chase required-run-rate or match-closeness component. Pressure is inferred from innings progression and wickets lost.

4

Comparability

IPL and T20I records are pooled. Competition context, opposition quality and venue are not fully normalised.

5

Availability

Player auction eligibility and IPL 2027 franchise availability are not certified by this performance model.

How to use this dashboard

Treat the lists as evidence-led screening outputs, not automatic auction decisions.

A

Start with role fit

Separate statistical rank from squad role and roster need.

B

Review the sample

Check high-pressure balls, matches and innings before trusting the score.

C

Validate externally

Use video, matchup, fitness, workload, availability and auction-register checks.

D

Keep uncertainty visible

Do not present exploratory bowler scores as a validated all-round bowling metric.

THE SCOUTING PRINCIPLE

Pressure reveals more than a highlight reel.

Use the numbers to identify candidates. Use context, video and role clarity to make the decision.
